nodes.question: In what contexts has the SES framework been found relevant?
nodes.answer: The SES framework has been found relevant in explaining sustainable outcomes in the management of forestry, fisheries, and water resources.
nodes.paragraph: This theory highlights the social, political and economic factors that influence ecological outcomes. Building on the foundations of social ecology theory, the socio-ecological systems (SES) framework provides a com- prehensive approach for examining waste dynamics within households, between households, and between household solid waste generators and the natural environment. This study explores waste management practices informed by local knowledge that support ecological system sustain- ability. The SES framework helps to identify key variables needed to understand both social and ecological systems, and how they interact with each other (Binder et al. 2013 , p. 15 of 20). By suggesting specific variables, the framework allows us to analyze the potential for sustainable develop- ment within these systems, providing a structured way to assess whether a social-ecological system can remain resil- ient and sustainable over time (Ostrom 2009, p. 420; Leslie et al. 2015, p. 5979). The SES framework has proven relevant in explaining sustainable outcomes in the management of forestry, fish- eries, and water resources (Bhatt et al. 2024; Binder et al.

nodes.question: What is the main focus of the paragraph regarding fisheries economic analysis?
nodes.answer: The main focus is on moving from a land-based economic analysis of fisheries to an integrated analysis that includes the entire seafood system value chain, incorporating global and local components and multi-stakeholder interests.
nodes.paragraph: 2003, 2008; Steenbeek et al. 2021; Stock et al. 2023). On the other hand, we need to move from the fisheries land-based economic analysis to an integrated analysis including the entire seafood system value chain (from fishers to consumers), where global and local components are included and multi-stakeholder interests are represented. In the last decades, several modelling tools have emerged to provide insights into the linkages of the ecological system with the anthropogenic pressures (Guisan and Zimmermann 2000; Fulton 2010), including marine ecosystem models such as Ecopath with Ecosim (EwE onwards).
